chapterNote: An ancient enmity resurfaces. Haman the Agagite — heir of Amalek, Israel's oldest foe — is raised to power, and one Jew's refusal to bow turns his wounded pride into a plan to exterminate a whole people. He casts lots for the day and buys a genocide by decree, sealed with the king's own ring into a law that cannot be recalled. The chapter ends with the two men drinking while the city reels: the calm of power that has just signed away thousands of lives.

1.text: After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, advancing him and setting his seat above all the officials who were with him.
1.notes: Agagite ties Haman to Agag, king of the Amalekites (1 Sam. 15), the people Israel was commanded to oppose from the days of the exodus. Mordecai the Benjamite descends from Kish — Saul's line, the very king who spared Agag. The private quarrel that follows is the flare-up of a war centuries old.

2.text: All the king's servants at the king's gate would kneel and bow low to Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai would not kneel or bow.
2.notes: The narrator does not spell out Mordecai's reason, but the Agagite name is the clue: this is not mere stubbornness but an old refusal to give an Amalekite the homage the king demands. Mordecai will name his Jewishness (v.4) as the ground of his stand.

3.text: Then the king's servants at the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why do you disobey the king's command?"

4.text: Day after day they spoke to him, and he would not listen; so they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai's stand would hold — for he had told them he was a Jew.

5.text: When Haman saw that Mordecai would not kneel or bow to him, he was filled with rage.

6.text: But he scorned to lay hands on Mordecai alone, for they had told him who Mordecai's people were; so Haman set out to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus.
6.amp: he disdained to strike Mordecai alone... he sought to annihilate [shamad (H8045) — to exterminate] all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, in the whole realm of Ahasuerus.
6.notes: Pride cannot be content with one man's death; it demands a people's. Haman's leap from a single slight to total extermination is the logic of every genocide, and Scripture exposes it in one merciless sentence.

7.text: In the first month, the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur (that is, the lot) before Haman, day after day and month after month, until it fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar.
7.notes: Pur is a Persian loanword; the Hebrew glosses it as 'the lot.' Haman leaves the killing-date to chance — but the lot lands nearly eleven months out, and that long delay is the very room the story needs for deliverance. 'The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD' (Prov. 16:33), a truth this godless-seeming book quietly enacts.

8.text: Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples in every province of your kingdom, whose laws differ from those of every other people and who do not keep the king's laws; it does not serve the king to leave them be.
8.notes: The oldest slander against the Jews, and against any minority: nameless ('a certain people'), everywhere, different, and disloyal. Haman never speaks the word 'Jew' to the king — only a faceless threat to order — and never mentions that his real grievance is one man who would not bow.

9.text: If it please the king, let it be written that they be destroyed, and I will weigh out ten thousand talents of silver into the hands of those who do the work, to bring into the king's treasuries."

10.text: The king drew the signet ring from his finger and handed it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the foe of the Jews.
10.notes: The signet ring is absolute authority: whatever is sealed with it becomes the king's own irrevocable word. Ahasuerus hands a genocide to 'the enemy of the Jews' without so much as asking the people's name — careless power arming malice.

11.text: "Keep the silver," the king said to Haman, "and the people too, to do with them as seems good to you."

12.text: Then the king's secretaries were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month, and it was all written down just as Haman ordered — to the king's satraps, to the governors over each province, and to the officials of each people, to every province in its own script and every people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's signet ring.

13.text: Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces, with the order to destroy, kill, and annihilate all the Jews — young and old, children and women — in a single day, the thirteenth of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, and to plunder their goods.
13.amp: to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate [le-hashmid la-harog ule-abbed — three verbs piled up for total extermination] all the Jews, young and old, little children and women, in one day.
13.notes: Three verbs for killing, heaped together, and the deliberate span 'young and old, children and women' — the decree spares no one. The date, the thirteenth of Adar, will become instead the day the Jews are delivered.

14.text: A copy of the writing was to be published as law in every province, made known to all the peoples, so that they would be ready for that day.

15.text: The couriers went out in haste at the king's command, and the decree was issued in the fortress of Susa. Then the king and Haman sat down to drink — but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.
15.notes: The closing image is unforgettable: two men calmly raising their cups while the capital around them recoils in bewilderment. Power at its ease over a death-warrant; the ordinary city sensing that something monstrous has been done.
